opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a big part of it was just curiosity about how much the landscape has changed. When AlphaGo came out, it felt like this monumental, almost unreachable achievement. You needed a huge team at DeepMind, enormous amounts of compute, and a lot of carefully engineered pieces. Then KataGo came along and showed that with smart algorithmic improvements, a much smaller effort could get to superhuman play far more efficiently. That was already a big step toward democratizing it.

What I wanted to know was how far that trend has gone. Today we have much better tooling, much cheaper compute, and, maybe most interestingly, AI coding assistants that can do a lot of the implementation grunt work. So the question in my head was: could one person, working mostly on weekends with modern tools, rebuild something in the spirit of AlphaGo from scratch? And what would that process teach me about where the real difficulty lies now?

There's also a pedagogical side. Go is a beautiful sandbox for thinking about search, reinforcement learning, and value estimation, all the ideas that are coming back into focus with reasoning models and test-time compute. Building it yourself forces you to understand every piece: how MCTS interacts with the policy and value networks, where training gets unstable, what actually matters versus what's folklore. You can read papers forever, but you don't really internalize the trade-offs until you've watched your own bot do something dumb and had to figure out why.

So it was part nostalgia, part a stress test of modern AI-assisted research workflows, and part a way to think more clearly about where search and learning are headed next.

r001.rationale: The response says improved tools, cheaper compute, and coding assistants made the work more accessible, and frames revisiting the project as testing how much easier it had become for one person.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the motivation was mostly embarrassment. KataGo exists, it's open source, it's superhuman, and in some sense the problem is "solved." So on paper there's no reason to build another Go bot. But I kept noticing that I didn't actually understand the thing end to end. I'd read the AlphaGo and AlphaZero papers, I could explain MCTS on a whiteboard, but I had never personally sat through the full loop of self-play, training, evaluation, and watching it fail in dumb ways for weeks. There's a big gap between "I understand this" and "I can make this work from scratch," and I wanted to close it.

The second reason is that Go is a really clean testbed for questions I care about in robotics. Robotics has all of this messiness around hardware, sensors, and data collection, and it's hard to tell whether your learning algorithm is bad or your gripper is bad. Go strips all that away. The environment is perfect, the simulator is free, and the only thing standing between you and a strong agent is your algorithm and your compute. So if I want to think clearly about scaling search versus scaling the policy, or how much a learned value function can substitute for lookahead, Go is a much more honest place to run those experiments than a robot arm.

And the third thing is that the tooling has changed so much since KataGo was written. It's much easier now to write the whole thing in a few hundred lines with modern frameworks, run it on a single box, and actually iterate. I was curious how much of the original engineering complexity was essential and how much was just an artifact of its era. Spoiler: a surprising amount of it turns out to still be essential, and that was itself a useful lesson.

r001.rationale: The candidate says modern tooling makes it much easier to build and iterate on a Go bot now, and that this change motivated revisiting the project.

astra-6.text: What interested me was whether you could get to strong play by a different route. KataGo already plays far beyond human level, so making a slightly stronger Go bot isn’t, by itself, that compelling. But Go gives you a clean setting to ask questions about learning and search: what does the model actually learn, and how much work does it still need to do at inference time? The motivation was to explore those questions, with Go as the test bed.

r001.rationale: The response says the motivation was to explore learning and inference-time search, but it does not identify an expectation that building a Go bot would become easier over time.

sol-6.1.text:
KataGo had already made it pretty clear that the interesting goal wasn’t just to build a stronger Go player. For me, the appeal was understanding the learning process: how do you start with a system that knows essentially nothing and get it to discover these very sophisticated strategies through self-play?

Go gives you this wonderfully clean setting where the rules are simple, you can generate your own training data, and you can measure progress. So revisiting it was a way to get my hands dirty with those ideas and build some intuition for what actually makes reinforcement learning work.

r001.rationale: The response says the motivation was to understand how self-play learning works and build intuition for reinforcement learning. It does not identify an expectation that building a Go bot would become easier over time.
